product.body_html:
[BUZZ RICKSON'S "BR11554" PEA-COAT “NAVAL CLOTHING FACTORY”]

It is said that the prototype for the coat commonly known as the "pea coat" existed as early as the 18th century.
The name is derived from the Dutch word "Piijekker"—"Pii" referring to a coarse woolen fabric and "jekker" to a jacket.
While various European militaries adopted pea-style coats, the specific model featured here is based on the version adopted by the U.S. Navy for enlisted personnel in the 1910s.
Key characteristics of the 1910s pea coat include the use of thick, high-density Melton wool and anchor buttons engraved with 13 stars representing the U.S. national emblem.
These 13 stars commemorate the original 13 states that existed when the United States gained independence in 1777.
Although the exact date the U.S. Navy adopted the pea coat is unknown, an overcoat for enlisted personnel was already listed in the uniform regulations during World War I.
The large collar was designed so that it could be turned up to cover the face and provide effective protection against strong winds while working at sea.
Additionally, the vertical slit pockets serve as hand-warmers to keep cold hands warm.
From the 1930s onwards, production efficiency and costs were re-evaluated; the fabric was made lighter, and the 13-star buttons were eventually discontinued.
The outer shell of this garment is made from 36-ounce high-density Melton wool, offering excellent protection against the cold.
This heavy, high-density wool provides superior insulation and wind resistance, making it an ideal choice for mid-winter outerwear.
The lining uses smooth rayon satin, ensuring the coat feels light and soft to wear despite its substantial, heavy-duty appearance. While the materials and construction stay true to vintage styles, the silhouette—including the body length and width—has been refined for a sleek, modern look.
Although the pea coat has military origins, it is now a quintessential autumn/winter outerwear staple that has firmly established itself as a go-to choice for city wear.
Its appeal lies in the exquisite balance between rugged, masculine military style and the refined elegance of high-quality fabric and tailoring.

This is a Buzz Rickson's fatigue jacket.
Commonly known as the "Jungle Fatigue" jacket—and officially designated the "Tropical Combat Uniform"—this garment was adopted and issued as field clothing for tropical environments during the Vietnam War in the early 1960s.
Although classified as a jacket, it is designed to be worn much like a shirt; it functions effectively as a lightweight outer layer or as an under-layer beneath a coat.
The material used is lightweight, quick-drying cotton poplin, selected specifically for tropical climates.
The design is an evolution of the parachute coat from World War II. These jackets are generally categorized into three types—early, mid, and late models—with the defining characteristic of the early model (the "First Model") being the exposed buttons on the pocket flaps.
This is a reproduction of that early model, featuring shoulder epaulets, exposed pocket buttons, and waist-adjustment tabs.
Designed for hot, humid environments, it utilizes cotton poplin—a relatively lightweight fabric often used for shirts, yet one that is densely woven, supple, and durable.
It also offers excellent moisture absorption and quick-drying properties.
Another distinctive feature is the angled chest pocket, which includes a pen slot and is positioned for easy access.
Sewn onto the jacket is a "joke patch" reflecting the anti-war sentiment that spread among U.S. troops during the conflict, alongside hand-embroidered details that express the soldiers' own sense of frustration and resignation regarding the war.
From our perspective, this garment is not merely a tribute to the military uniform itself; rather, it recreates the image of a soldier's personal emotions erupting over the "uniform provided by the state."
It is a jacket born from the atmosphere of anti-war and war-weary sentiment that permeated the U.S. military as the Vietnam War dragged on. While it bears a clear anti-war message like "MAKE LOVE NOT WAR," it also features a brand of dark, soldier-style humor—"PEACE THE OLD FASHIONED WAY" (creating peace by bombing with B-52s)—that could be interpreted as the exact opposite.
The famous phrase "Fighter by day / Lover by night / Drunkard by choice / Army by mistake" feels less like a statement of political anti-war ideology and more like an expression of soldier culture—a way of laughing at oneself for "ending up in a place like this."

One might be tempted to simply lump this together with other "anti-war jackets," but I felt it was something far more human than that label implies.
What this jacket conveys may be the "honest feelings of a soldier" rather than an "ideology."
"I hate war. But I’m a soldier. I like girls. I want to drink. Joining the army was a mistake. MAKE LOVE NOT WAR." Yet, at the same time, they joke about creating "old-fashioned peace" with B-52s.
They even poke fun at the very war they are fighting in, calling it the "SOUTH EAST ASIA WAR GAMES."
It doesn't neatly align with a single ideology; that lack of neatness is precisely what makes this jacket feel so real.

There is no simple way to explain the emotions of someone who has actually been on the battlefield.
There is fear. Resignation. Perhaps even pride. There is drinking and joking. There is the longing to go home. I feel like all of those things are mixed together in this jacket.
Taking all of that into account, the phrase "a sense of helpless frustration"—used by the manufacturer to describe it—captures the essence of this jacket perfectly.
Furthermore, the fact that we can also appreciate such a jacket as a cool fashion item feels, in many ways, deeply human—giving the jacket a rich, complex character.

This A-2, bearing contract number AC18091, comes from the second production lot by Rough Wear—a company that supplied the military with A-2 jackets on five separate occasions.
It features the company's signature pattern design, including a stand collar and a unique construction where a symmetrical body pattern—originally not designed for a front placket—was adapted to incorporate one.
This specific version is a "no-stencil" type, meaning it lacks the Air Force insignia typically found on the shoulder.
While military regulations of the time specified horsehide for A-2 jackets, this particular lot utilized goatskin—a rarity for the A-2—likely due to procurement circumstances.
Goatskin is often associated with the Navy's iconic G-1 leather jacket; however, because goatskin hides have a smaller surface area compared to horsehide, manufacturers were compelled to cut the leather into smaller pieces—much like with the G-1—to ensure efficient, waste-free usage.
When cutting goatskin for a pattern like the A-2, which requires a single large piece of leather for the back, the remaining scraps offer limited utility for other components.
In other words, this represents a highly luxurious use of the material.
The leather itself is a carefully selected, thick goatskin; it is vegetable-tanned and base-dyed, then layered with additional dyes—starting from lighter shades—to create a natural, nuanced color variation.
For the final finish, artisans meticulously rub in solid wax while applying heat to melt it into the leather.
This process allows the base color to show through when viewed in sunlight, resulting in a rich, deep hue.
With its beautifully pronounced vertical grain, this jacket is a piece that truly captivates the wearer with the unique appeal of goatskin.

All we had on hand were the heart-shaped buttons...

That is where we started. The reason is simple: it was a jacket I had always wanted to make.
And of course, I felt that if I was going to do it, it *had* to feature those heart-shaped buttons.
We referenced the vintage overalls for the fabric and the "MASTER CLOTH" label.
For the warp, we used a #7 yarn with natural, subtle slubs—avoiding an artificial look—while the weft uses a finer #16 yarn with a slightly lower thread count. By using a weft yarn that is finer than the warp, the uneven texture of the warp yarn stands out prominently; this results in a 10oz 2x1 denim fabric that produces distinct vertical fading.
For the color, we deliberately chose 100% synthetic indigo without any additives.
The number of dyeing dips is lower than that of 1920s "XX Denim," resulting in a brighter shade.

For those who already own a TCB coverall and are wondering about the texture of this new fabric:
It is slightly softer than the fabric used for the Tabby's Jacket, though the blue hue is similar.
The twill weave is clearly visible despite the 2x1 construction, and the unevenness of the warp yarns is apparent to the eye; compared to the Black Cat Jacket or Tabby's Jacket, you can expect the kind of rugged fading characteristic of vintage garments.
What is the basis for this Chore Coat?
I own a couple of vintage pieces from the 1940s and 50s.

If I were to encounter an actual vintage piece in the future, there might be differences from what I’ve imagined.
It’s the reverse of a sci-fi movie depicting the future; this is a Chore Coat created by envisioning the past. If a time machine is invented in the future, I’d like to wear this coat and travel back to the 1920s.
I look forward to seeing if I’d get found out as a time traveler.

Thermal fabric is a staple for cold-weather tops, generally categorized into two types based on the knit structure: waffle and honeycomb.
This particular item features a waffle knit; it is crafted using thick yarn on a low-gauge machine, resulting in a large, pronounced texture—hence the name "Big Waffle."
The textured surface traps warm air, providing excellent heat retention.
Despite the fabric's substantial, voluminous feel, it offers just the right amount of stretch, ensuring exceptional comfort.
